items.article: The mint flavor of San Francisco's favorite It's-It ice cream cookie sandwiches has changed color. A major change has come for San Francisco’s beloved It’s-It ice cream sandwiches. The mint flavor of the ice cream cookie sandwich , once an ostentatiously loud shade of green, has changed color, as first spotted by the San Francisco Chronicle. (The Chronicle and SFGATE are both owned by Hearst but have separate newsrooms.) An SFGATE editor bought a box at Andronico’s and confirmed the breaking news — the bright, toothpaste-green ice cream had been drained of color, with a far more muted, pale pastel green in its place. Where the shade once screamed “GREEN!” at the top of its lungs, now, it only whispered. Curiously, though, It’s-It has mostly kept the change quiet. Despite SFGATE’s repeated attempts this week to reach the Burlingame-based company for comment, It’s-It never got back to us. The company has not released any statement announcing the change to its customers, and photos of the mint ice cream sandwich on its website remain the same , advertising the old seafoam green color instead of the new, lighter shade. It’s-It President Charles Shamieh did speak with the Chronicle, telling the outlet that It’s-It made the change due to U.S. Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. items.article: Smit Machchhar says in video call with Indian PM that he realised if he did not get up ‘passengers would lose their lives’ The Indian pilot who helped thwart an apparent attempt to crash a flydubai flight to Tel Aviv said his faith and his desire to save his passengers allowed him to make a “last push” to open the cockpit door as he fought for his life. Capt Smit Machchhar, who was recovering in an Abu Dhabi hospital, described to India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, how he helped save the plane and its more than 170 passengers. “I had suffered so many injuries that I had collapsed. At that time, I could feel that the aircraft was going down. I knew this was the last push,” Machchhar told Modi in a video call on Friday. “I was fighting for my life. At one point, I realised that if I didn’t get up … then passengers would lose their lives.” His Omani co-pilot apparently stabbed him and set the plane on a steep descent, with the aircraft plummeting about 17,000 feet in the span of a minute. While still being attacked, Machchhar managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers to enter, subdue the attacker and ultimately stabilise the plane. The full circumstances of the attack are still under investigation, but a relief crew on the flight helped land the plane safely in Tabouk, north-west Saudi Arabia . items.article: The UAE is leading the investigation, while Saudi Arabia has conducted preliminary inquiries and Israeli investigators are expected to take part. The September 30 cockpit attack on a Flydubai flight bound for Tel Aviv has been described as an act of terrorism by a senior UAE official and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. However, the investigation is still underway to establish the motive and determine whether there were any outside links. The probe is focusing on whether the incident was a deliberate act of terrorism, a planned attempt to bring down the aircraft or an attack carried out by the co-pilot acting alone. The UAE is leading the investigation, while Saudi Arabia has conducted preliminary inquiries and Israeli investigators are expected to take part. No final finding has yet been made on the motive or on any outside involvement. The incident took place on Wednesday aboard Flydubai Flight FZ1073, which was carrying more than 170 people. While the aircraft was flying over Saudi Arabia, the co-pilot allegedly attacked and stabbed the captain, causing the Boeing 737 to enter a steep descent. The flight was later diverted to Tabuk in Saudi Arabia, where it landed safely after passengers and crew intervened. items.article: As the weather gets colder, rats and mice are more likely to venture into our homes - but pest control experts say there are a few simple steps you can take to keep them out There's nothing quite like the dread that washes over you when you spot tiny droppings on the floor or open your cupboards to find chewed-up packaging. Unless, of course, you come face to face with an actual mouse or rat . October signals the start of peak rodent season across the UK. As temperatures fall and food sources grow scarce , these unwanted pests are far more likely to make their way into your home. After being both inspired and thoroughly disgusted by spotting a mouse in my kitchen in the middle of the night recently, I decided to seek out advice from pest control experts on the most effective ways to keep them at bay. Before taking any action, it's essential to establish whether you actually have a rodent infestation on your hands.
